 This woman made $200 million. And all her stock trades are public for you to copy. Here's what the research says about copying her trades, where to find them, and if it's actually a good idea. The truth might surprise you. Her name is Nancy Pelosi. By law, members of Congress must publicly report their stock trades and their spouses within 45 days. You can read them all on the House Clerk's website. Let's examine one trade, posted by a copy trading app. July 28th. Her husband buys Bloom Energy at about $167. The report came August 21st. By then, the stock was up 21% before anyone could copy it. And this one kept climbing. But winning trades are the ones that get posted by these platforms. So was that just luck? Let's look at the record. A 2026 study took all 35 stock purchases in the household's record, each held for 300 trading days. On average, they rose 33%. 15.6% better than the market. But 35 trades is a small sample. A few huge winners can lift the average by luck alone. Statisticians test for that. This result does not pass. And compared with what? Did you buy giant tech companies while giant tech beats the market? Are you a great stock picker? Or did a rising tide lift all ships? More than half the purchases were in the 10 largest companies in the market. Those 10 rose 27.6%. And two Nvidia purchases did most of the work. They beat the market by 186 and 122%. Against similar stocks, same size and type, the picks came out 1.3% behind. That's not a loss. They rose 33%. Similar stocks just rose a little more. Now all of Congress. Copy on the day of the trade, plus 13.8%. Copy from the report about a month later, 13.6%. So copying works? Not quite. The market made 1.7% more. You made money just less than buying the whole market and doing nothing. So, the posts are real. You decide if they're cherry picked. So, is it a good idea? The gains came from owning the biggest stocks. And copying Congress did worse than simply holding the market. In trading, the data holds the truth the headline hides. That's why multi-billion dollar hedge funds don't copy Nancy Pelosi. But they do copy trades, all the time. Sourced from proprietary data sets or inferred from market dynamics.
